items.title: The Twenty-Two Marks Complete: What Remains Undone Even After the Absorptions

items.zh: 謂時時間諮受讀誦論量決擇，勤修善品，如是乃應受他信施；又樂遠離，以正方便修諸作意；又復晝夜，於退分、勝分二法，知斷修習；又於生死見大過失；又於涅槃見勝功德。
items.en: Regularly seeking instruction, reading, reciting, discussing, and discerning the teaching, diligently cultivating what is wholesome — only thus does one deserve to receive others' faithful offerings. Delighting in seclusion, applying right effort to the stages of meditative attention. Day and night, recognising and severing what causes decline while cultivating what brings genuine progress. Seeing the great fault in saṃsāra. And seeing the surpassing virtue in nirvāṇa.

items.zh: 由此五相，是名第三處觀察。如是精勤修善品者，略為四苦之所隨逐。謂於四沙門果，未能隨有所證故，猶為惡趣苦所隨逐。體是生老病死法故，為內壞苦之所隨逐。一切所愛離別法故，為愛壞苦之所隨逐。自業所作故，一切苦因之所隨逐。彼為如是四苦隨逐，應以七相審正觀察。由此七相，是名第四處觀察。彼於如是四處，以二十二相正觀察時，便生如是如理作意：謂我為求如是事故，誓受下劣形相威儀及資身具，誓受禁戒，誓受精勤常修善法；而我今者於四種苦為脫何等？若我如是自策自勵，誓受三處，猶為四苦常所隨逐，未得解脫；我今不應為苦隨逐，未於勝定獲得自在，中路止息，或復退屈。如是精勤如理作意，乃得名為出家之想及沙門想。彼於圓滿修多方便以為依止，由世間道，證得三摩地圓滿故；於煩惱斷，猶未證得，復依樂斷，常勤修習。又彼已得善世間道，數數為得三摩地自在故；依止樂修無間而轉。又於正信長者、居士、婆羅門等，獲得種種利養恭敬，而不依此利養恭敬，而生貪著。亦不於他利養恭敬，及餘不信婆羅門等，對面、背面諸不可意身業、語業現行事中，心生憤恚，又復於彼無損害心。又愛、慢、見、無明、疑惑種種定中諸隨煩惱不復現行，善守念住。又非證得勝奢摩他，即以如是奢摩他故，謂己一切所作已辦；亦不向他說己所證。彼由如是樂斷樂修，心無貪恚，正念現前，離增上慢。於諸衣服隨宜獲得，便生喜足。如於衣服，於餘飲食、臥具等喜足，當知亦爾。又正了知而為受用。謂如是等諸資生具，但為治身令不敗壞，暫止饑渴，攝受梵行，廣說乃至於食知量。
items.en: By these five aspects, this is called the examination of the third domain. One who thus diligently cultivates wholesome qualities is, in brief, followed by four kinds of suffering. Because one has not yet attained any of the four fruits of the ascetic life, one is still followed by the suffering of the bad destinies. Because one's very nature is subject to birth, old age, sickness and death, one is followed by the suffering of inner decay. Because everything one loves is subject to separation, one is followed by the suffering of the loss of what is loved. Because of what one's own actions have produced, one is followed by the causes of all suffering. Followed by these four sufferings, one should carefully and correctly examine them through seven aspects. By these seven aspects, this is called the examination of the fourth domain. When one thus correctly examines these four domains through twenty-two aspects, proper attention of this kind arises: 'For the sake of seeking this very goal I have vowed to take on a lowly appearance, deportment and requisites for supporting the body; I have vowed to take on the precepts; I have vowed to take on diligence and the constant cultivation of wholesome qualities. Yet now, from which of the four sufferings have I been freed? If, though I spur and urge myself on in this way and have vowed to take on the three domains, I am still constantly followed by the four sufferings and have not yet been freed, then I ought not now, while still followed by suffering and before gaining mastery over superior concentration, stop halfway or fall back in discouragement.' Only diligent, proper attention of this kind deserves to be called the perception of one gone forth and the perception of an ascetic. Relying on the many means for cultivating perfection, one has attained the perfecting of concentration through the mundane path; but not yet having attained the abandonment of the afflictions, one further relies on delight in abandoning and constantly cultivates with diligence. Further, having already attained the wholesome mundane path, in order to attain mastery over concentration again and again, one relies on delight in cultivation and proceeds without interruption. Further, although one obtains all kinds of gain and honour from elders, householders, brahmins and others with right faith, one does not depend on this gain and honour, nor become attached to it. Nor does one's mind become indignant at the gain and honour of others, or at the disagreeable bodily and verbal actions of other brahmins and the like who lack faith, whether done to one's face or behind one's back; and one has no intention of harming them. Further, the various secondary afflictions in concentration — craving, conceit, views, ignorance and doubt — no longer occur, and one guards the establishment of mindfulness well. Further, having attained superior calm-abiding, one does not on account of that calm-abiding consider that everything to be done has been done, nor does one tell others what one has attained. Through this delight in abandoning and delight in cultivation, the mind is free from greed and anger, right mindfulness is present, and one is free of overestimation of oneself. Whatever clothing one obtains, one is content with it. As with clothing, so it should be understood with food and drink, bedding and seats and the rest. Further, one makes use of them with correct understanding: that is, such requisites of life are only for maintaining the body so that it does not decay, for temporarily allaying hunger and thirst, and for supporting the holy life, and so on in full, up to knowing moderation in eating.

items.title: Mastery Achieved: Five Further Practices, and Branch Six Closes Entirely

items.zh: 彼由如是正修行故，於三摩地獲得自在。依止彼故，其心清白，無有瑕穢，離隨煩惱，廣說乃至獲得不動，能引一切勝神通慧。
items.en: Through practising correctly in this way, one attains mastery over concentration. Resting on this, the mind becomes pure and unstained, free of secondary afflictions, reaching what is called "the unmoving," able to give rise to every kind of superior wisdom born of paranormal insight.

items.zh: 是名三摩地自在。此三摩地自在廣義，當知唯有如所說相。除此更無若過若增。又先所說得三摩地，若中所說三摩地圓滿，及今所說三摩地自在，總名無上世間一切種清淨。當知此清淨，唯在正法，非諸外道。
items.en: This is called mastery over concentration. The full meaning of this mastery over concentration should be understood to consist only of the characteristics as stated. Beyond this, there is nothing further to exceed it, and nothing further to add. Further, the attainment of concentration explained first, the perfecting of concentration explained in the middle, and the mastery over concentration now explained are together called unsurpassed mundane purity of every kind. It should be understood that this purity exists only within the true teaching, and not among the non-Buddhist teachers.

items.title: The Seventh and Final Branch Opens: Supramundane Purity in Five Stages

items.zh: 云何出世間一切種清淨？當知略有五種。何等為五？一、入聖諦現觀；二、入聖諦現觀已，離諸障礙；三、入聖諦現觀已，為欲證得速疾通慧，作意思惟諸歡喜事；四、修習如所得道；五、證得極清淨道，及果功德。
items.en: What is supramundane purity of every kind? It should be known, in brief, to be fivefold. What are the five? Entering direct realisation of the noble truths; having entered that realisation, removing every remaining obstacle; having entered that realisation, applying the mind to what brings genuine joy in order to attain swift, penetrating wisdom; cultivating the path already attained; and attaining the utterly pure path together with its fruit of merit.

items.zh: 云何入聖諦現觀？謂有如來諸弟子眾，已善修習世間清淨，知長夜中，由妙五欲積集其心。食所持故，長養其心，於彼諸欲生愛樂故，而於諸欲深見過患。於上勝境，見寂靜德。
items.en: What is entering direct realisation of the noble truths? It means that the assembly of the Tathāgata's disciples, having already cultivated mundane purity well, know that throughout the long night their minds have been built up by the fine sense pleasures; sustained by them as by food, the mind has been nourished, and delight in those sense pleasures has arisen. Yet now they see deeply the danger in sense pleasures, and in the higher, superior states they see the virtue of peace.

blocks.text: The long reflection on the four places concludes; mastery of concentration is reached; and the seventh branch, **supramundane purity**, begins. The middle of today's reading is a long passage **missing from Ru-Yi's translation** (0392a27–c02); the English column gives our own translation, and the commentary summarises it.
One reflects on the vow of constant diligence in the good, in five ways.

items: **The fourth place: four sufferings.** Even a diligent renunciant is still followed by four sufferings: the danger of bad destinies, since no fruit of the path is yet attained; birth, ageing, sickness, and death; separation from all that is loved; and the results of one's own deeds.

**The right attitude.** One reflects: "I took this humble form, these precepts, this diligence, to be free of suffering; and I am still followed by four sufferings. I must not stop halfway or fall back before mastering concentration." This, the treatise says, is the real meaning of "the perception of a renunciant" and "the perception of an ascetic".

**How such a person lives.** Delighting in abandoning and in cultivating; not attached to offerings, nor angry at disrespect from others; not overcome by the subtle afflictions of concentration; not thinking that calm alone means the work is done, and not telling others of one's attainments; content with whatever robes, food, and lodging come; using them only to sustain the body for the holy life.

blocks.text: Mastery is completed by five further practices, and the mind is no longer shaken by the "eight disturbances": pain, pleasure, sorrow, joy, examination, analysis, out-breath, and in-breath (Master Cháng Bǎi). The sixth branch, mundane purity, is complete.

The seventh and last branch has five stages: entering the direct realisation of the truths; removing obstacles after that; applying the mind to the matters of joy, for swift penetrating wisdom; cultivating the path already attained; and reaching the fruit of utmost purity. Master Cháng Bǎi: "swift penetrating wisdom" here should be read as the exhaustion of the corruptions.

quiz.q: After mastery, "up to reaching the unmoving" — what does Master Cháng Bǎi say "unmoving" means?
options: the eight disturbances — pain, pleasure, sorrow, joy, examination, analysis, out-breath, in-breath — cannot shake the fourth absorption
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the eight disturbances are pain, pleasure, sorrow, joy, examination, analysis, out-breath, and in-breath; none of these can shake, disturb, or harm the fourth absorption. He adds that the powers here are the five other than the exhaustion of corruptions.

quiz.q: What five stages of supramundane purity does the treatise name?
options: entering realisation of the truths; removing obstacles; reflecting on matters of joy for swift wisdom; cultivating the path attained; attaining the path and fruit of utmost purity
quiz.why: The treatise lists five: entering direct realisation of the noble truths; after that, removing obstacles; applying the mind to matters of joy to attain swift penetrating wisdom; cultivating the path attained; and attaining the utterly pure path with its fruit. Master Cháng Bǎi: this explains, for śrāvakas, the path from stream-entry to arhatship.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi read "swift penetrating wisdom" differently in mundane versus supramundane purity?
options: in mundane purity it can mean the wisdom of psychic powers; in supramundane purity it should mean the exhaustion of corruptions
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: to achieve swift penetrating wisdom is the exhaustion of corruptions — here it should be read that way. In the mundane section, following Venerable Miào Jìng, the wisdom of psychic powers suffices.
